title: The reason most people never test their own setups has nothing to do with the setup
author: person-person12
selftext:
Say you trade an opening range breakout on NQ. Fifteen minute range, long on the break, stop under the range low. Ten seconds to explain to another trader.

Now find out whether it has ever actually worked.

You need intraday history going back far enough to mean something, which is where most people stop, because yfinance caps out around 90 days and real intraday data is a subscription. Then you need to walk it candle by candle without letting the strategy peek at the next candle, which is easy to get wrong and impossible to notice when you do. Then fills, costs, and something at the end that tells you more than a win rate.

**That gap is the whole reason the average trader never tests anything they do.** Not laziness. The setup is the easy part and everything around it is a second job.

What I use now is [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca). I describe the rules the way I would to another trader, it writes the Python, and it runs on history thats already sitting there. **1,776 US stocks and ETFs back to 2000, and NQ, ES, GC and SI from 2016**, one minute up to daily. No data subscription and no API key of my own.

What comes back is every individual trade, the equity curve, drawdown, profit factor, a regime breakdown, and a Monte Carlo that reshuffles the trade order so you can see how much of the result was sequence luck rather than edge.

And most ideas fail it. Mine included. I tested a setup that was all over my feed a couple of weeks ago, it won **60% of its trades and still lost money**, because the average loser was 1.5x the average winner. A percentage on its own told me nothing. The trade list told me everything.

If something does survive, the same rules can go out as a TradingView indicator or run on your own broker inside limits you set, without being rebuilt.

The part that surprised me was how fast it kills ideas I was sure about.
